Murmured
MUR-merd
v. (past)
From Latin murmurare, to make a low sound; the word is onomatopoeic. Webster 1828: to grumble; to complain; to utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice. In Scripture it is the characteristic sin of the wilderness generation, and the New Testament forbids it to the church by name.

Biblical Definition

Murmured is the wilderness verb. Three days out of the Red Sea, the people murmured against Moses, saying, What shall we drink? (Exodus 15:24). At the wilderness of Sin the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron (Exodus 16:2). After Korah’s judgment, all the congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and against Aaron, saying, Ye have killed the people of the LORD (Numbers 16:41). And God treats it as directed at Himself: Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness… which have murmured against me (Numbers 14:29). Deuteronomy records what murmuring actually says when it is quoted: ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt (Deuteronomy 1:27) — the recasting of deliverance as malice. The psalm summarizes: But murmured in their tents, and hearkened not unto the voice of the LORD (Psalm 106:25). In the Gospels the Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven (John 6:41). Paul makes the wilderness the church’s warning: Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer (1 Corinthians 10:10).

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster 1828 defines MURMUR as a low sound continued or continually repeated; and, as a verb, to grumble, to complain, to utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice. The half-articulated quality is exactly the sin’s character.

expand to see more

MURMUR, n. — A low sound continued or continually repeated, as that of a stream running in a stony channel.

A complaint half suppressed, or uttered in a low, muttering voice.

MURMUR, v.i. — To utter complaints in a low, half-articulated voice; to grumble; to express discontent.

The definition catches what makes murmuring so hard to deal with pastorally. It is not open rebellion, which can be answered, but a low continual sound in the tents that never becomes an argument anyone has to defend.

Key Scripture

Exodus 16:2 — "And the whole congregation of the children of Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron in the wilderness:"

Numbers 14:29 — "Your carcases shall fall in this wilderness; and all that were numbered of you, according to your whole number, from twenty years old and upward, which have murmured against me,"

Deuteronomy 1:27 — "And ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us, he hath brought us forth out of the land of Egypt, to deliver us into the hand of the Amorites, to destroy us."

John 6:41 — "The Jews then murmured at him, because he said, I am the bread which came down from heaven."

1 Corinthians 10:10 — "Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured, and were destroyed of the destroyer."

Modern Corruption

Murmuring is corrupted into a virtue wherever complaint is renamed as honesty, authenticity, or the healthy processing of disappointment — and 1 Corinthians 10:10 shows the apostolic estimate of it.

expand to see more

Numbers 14:29 makes the decisive point: Israel murmured against Moses and Aaron, and God says they murmured against me. Complaint about circumstances is complaint about the Providence that arranged them, whatever name it travels under. The contemporary permission to vent, to be raw, to say the unedited thing as though sincerity sanctified it, has no footing in these chapters. Scripture provides an abundant vocabulary for honest grief before God — the psalms of lament are in the canon and are meant to be prayed — but a lament is addressed to God and ends in trust, while a murmur is spoken in the tents about Him. Deuteronomy 1:27 quotes what it actually said: Because the LORD hated us. That is the theology inside every murmur.

Paul’s warning in 1 Corinthians 10:10 is addressed to a church, not to Israel, and the whole passage says these things are written for our admonition, upon whom the ends of the world are come. The remedy he gives elsewhere is startlingly absolute: Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Philippians 2:14) — and the verse before it grounds the possibility in grace, it is God which worketh in you both to will and to do of his good pleasure. A congregation where discontent circulates quietly is not merely unpleasant; it is repeating the sin for which a generation’s carcases fell in the wilderness. Isaiah adds the hope: they that murmured shall learn doctrine (Isaiah 29:24). The cure for a murmuring people is teaching.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

The Hebrew verb is lun, to lodge or to grumble — the same root as spending the night, which is why murmuring in Scripture is done in tents. The Greek gogguzo is itself an imitation of the sound.

expand to see more

Hebrew lun (H3885) — to lodge, to pass the night, and in a related form to murmur or grumble; Exodus 15:24, 16:2, Numbers 14:29.

Hebrew ragan (H7279) — to backbite, to murmur; ye murmured in your tents (Deuteronomy 1:27; Psalm 106:25).

Greek gogguzo (G1111) — to mutter, murmur; an onomatopoeic verb (John 6:41; 1 Corinthians 10:10).

Greek goggusmos (G1112) — murmuring; Do all things without murmurings and disputings (Philippians 2:14).

The overlap of lun as lodging and grumbling is not accidental in the narrative: the murmuring is done in the tents, at night, out of Moses’ hearing.

Usage

"Which have murmured against me (Numbers 14:29) — God receives complaint against His servants as complaint against Himself."

"Ye murmured in your tents, and said, Because the LORD hated us (Deuteronomy 1:27) — the theology hidden inside a murmur, quoted back."

"Neither murmur ye, as some of them also murmured (1 Corinthians 10:10) — the wilderness written for the church’s admonition."
